fragments.text: Thank you so much to Janesco and the information for all program working group on information accessibility for the opportunity to speak at this year's conference. I'm so honored to be joining you today to commemorate the International Day for Universal Access to Information. My name is Monica Desai and I'm head of the Global Connectivity and Access Policy Team at Facebook. My team covers issues involving accessibility, online messaging, online video, infrastructure, net neutrality, and spectrum. Prior to joining Facebook, I spent over a decade in senior positions at the United States Federal Communications Commission, including as Chief of the Consumer and Governmental Affairs Bureau, which develops all policies and rules in connection with accessibility. I later served as Chief of the Media Bureau, which has oversight over broadcasters in cable companies and overseas captioning policies.

I was also a partner at a law firm where my practice included counseling clients on accessibility matters. This is all to say that accessibility has been a significant part of my career, which is why I'm so happy to work at Facebook, a company that is constantly working to improve the accessibility of our products and diversity and inclusion in our workforce. Facebook's mission is to give people the power to build community and bring the world closer together, and that includes people with disabilities. We have seen that hundreds of millions of people need or choosing to use accessibility tools to experience the information and the connections that happen on Facebook. So making our products accessible to persons with disabilities is really critical to getting our mission right.

We've built a variety of tools to enhance access to our services. Facebook has a dedicated centralized accessibility team to define, develop, and distribute user accessibility requirements, training, best practices, tools, technologies, metrics, and other support to advance accessibility work within the company. This means that accessibility is embedded into the different departments that touch the product lifecycle. This includes design, research, and engineering, as well as policy and legal, which results in an important cross-functional effort to promote accessibility in our products. So with that background, I'd like to talk about some of the ways that Facebook is using artificial intelligence to improve accessibility at scale, including through our automatic photo description technology and automated captioning.

I know AI for accessibility is key for this audience. I'll then highlight some recent accessibility progress that might be interesting to you, and I'll also touch on our Workplace initiative supporting people with disabilities. First, how are you using artificial intelligence to promote accessibility? In 2016, we launched the first version of our automatic photo description technology called automatic alt text or AAT. This is an AI-driven tool that uses object recognition to generate a description of photos that enable people to using screen readers to hear a list of items that photos may contain. And earlier this year, we introduced the next generation of AAT, which can now recognize over 1,200 concepts, objects and places, which is more than 10 times as many as the earlier generation.

The new concepts include highly requested ones like landmarks and more types of sports, breeds of dogs, and various types of foods. The updated AAT can also provide additional context about a photo, such as the count of the recognized objects, positional information, and a comparison of the relative prominence of objects in an image. The updated AAT is only possible through technology advances that combine advanced artificial intelligence and computer vision. AAT was originally developed using human-label data I could recognize 100 concepts. In the updated AAT, we trained our AI model by sampling billions of public Facebook and Instagram images and translated hashtags from 15 different countries across five continents. The new approach gave us the ability to more readily repurpose machine learning models as the starting point for training on new tasks, also known as transfer learning.

This enabled us to create models that identified concepts like landmarks and food types that wouldn't have been possible in the past. For richer information like position and object counts, we trained an efficient and faster object detection model that can recognize and localize 1,200 concepts using detectron to go, an open source platform for object detection, and segmentation developed by Facebook AI research. As we consulted with screen reader users regarding AAT and how best to improve it, they made it clear that accuracy is paramount. To that end, we've included only those concepts for which we could ensure well-trained models that met a certain high threshold of precision. There is a margin for error, which is why we start every AAT description with maybe we've set the bar very high and have intentionally omitted concepts that we could not reliably identify.

So we built AAT to bridge this gap. As of August, more than 80% of images displayed on Facebook and Instagram contain automatic alt text. And alt text descriptions are available in 45 different languages, helping ensure that it's useful to people around the world. Next, I'd like to talk about how we've used AI to expand the availability of closed captioning. Several years ago, Facebook enabled users to manually add captions for video and to customize those caption displays to the user. We recognize that not everyone takes time to add captions and our goal is for every video to have them. So we committed to making large investments in AI and leveraging it to enable automated captioning for video. Automated captioning makes it simple and easy for creators to add captions.

Captions are generated with the press of a button and can be reviewed by content creators and edited so that they have full control. And we strongly believe it is one of the best ways to make captions available for videos on Facebook. Automated captioning is available for Facebook ads and pages, Facebook Live, Workplace Live, and Instagram TV to for support and the availability of captioning together along with the manual captioning tools that I mentioned. I'd also like to talk about some of Facebook's other recent accessibility advances. You may be aware that Facebook produces the Oculus line of VR products. We released Oculus version 30 recently and that includes new accessibility features to make the future of computing a better experience for everyone.

We're constantly exploring new ways to make VR more inclusive and with version 30 we're introducing a brand new accessibility tab into the Oculus settings menu. There you'll find tools and features that enable you to customize your VR experience. We've moved some existing features under the new accessibility tab such as the ability to change your headsets default text size, but we're adding two new features with version 30 as well. The first is color correction, a system level display setting that increases legibility of colors that are commonly difficult to differentiate. The second much requested feed new feature enables you to experience VR from a standing vantage point even while you're sitting this raise view feature raises your viewing height by 16 inches or point four meters in apps that support this function.

Investing in the future in 2020 Facebook reality labs announced our responsible innovation principles to guide our work as we build the next computing platform. As part of this commitment, we also announced two requests for proposal to research the impact of AR VR and smart device technology.

And just last month, we announced the 13 awardees who will receive $75,000 in funding for their research. We're excited to share that the list of awardees includes a number of research projects focused on accessible AR VR. We also launched a voice assisted camera feature for WhatsApp that makes it easier for people who are blind and visually impaired to take photos. It works with the screen reader on iOS devices so you can hear verbal clues when a face is in the frame of the viewfinder and you can use this in more than 30 languages. In keeping with our privacy commitments, we don't log any information about who uses this feature and we don't know whose face is in the frame.

All images taken with the WhatsApp camera are sent into end encrypted so that only the sender and the recipient have access to them. And last year, we completely reengineered Facebook.com and were able to integrate greater accessibility into the website. We reorganized and expanded heading markup and revamped keyboard shortcuts to help people using screen readers better understand what's on a page and find what interests them more quickly. I'm going to close with a few notes on disability inclusion in a hiring at Facebook. We recognize that building products that are accessible requires a workforce that can represent and advocate for the diversity of our users. At Facebook, disability inclusion is one of our top priorities.

Our recruiting and accommodations team offers support to candidates through the hiring process. And once they're hired, our accommodations program supports employees with disabilities. We also have an active employee resource group for people with disabilities. Indeed, Facebook has been named one of the best places to work for disability inclusion three years in a row by the American Association of Persons with disabilities and disability in disability equality index.
